title: SQL as a Working Skill
eyebrow: Data fluency · Ask precise questions and change data safely
summary: Learn SQL by tracing rows through filtering, grouping, joining, changing, and transaction boundaries, then apply those skills to indexes, nulls, debugging, migrations, and production safety.
prerequisites: The 7 Types of Databases introduces relational data, constraints, transactions, and indexes; this guide practices SQL itself.
APIs and Data Exchange helps explain how application code sends a query and receives rows.
learningOutcomes: Translate a question into a query whose filtering, joining, grouping, and ordering are explicit.
Predict how NULL, duplicate rows, aggregate functions, and join choices affect results.
Change relational data safely with transactions, parameterized queries, constrained migrations, and evidence from query plans.

heroVisual.title: A query transforms a relation into an answer
heroVisual.caption: SQL describes the result you want; the database parses, plans, executes, and returns rows while enforcing its rules.

nodes.label: Question
nodes.detail: Name the facts, relationships, filters, and ordering the result needs.

nodes.label: Relations
nodes.detail: Tables expose rows and columns governed by keys and constraints.

nodes.label: Query
nodes.detail: SELECT, FROM, JOIN, WHERE, grouping, and ordering describe a result.

nodes.label: Plan
nodes.detail: The database chooses access and join strategies for the query.

nodes.label: Rows or change
nodes.detail: The system returns a result or commits/rejects a data modification.

sections.title: 1. Turn a question into a precise result
sections.summary: SQL skill begins before syntax: define one row's meaning and the evidence the answer must contain.

blocks.text: Suppose a support team asks, 'Which open tickets belong to customers in Germany, newest first?' That question names a result shape: one ticket per row, a relationship to a customer, filters on status and country, and descending creation time. Write those choices down before combining clauses; otherwise a query can run successfully while answering a different question.

blocks.title: Describe the result before writing SQL

items.title: Define the row
items.explanation: Say what one output row represents: ticket, customer, invoice, or an aggregate such as one row per month.
items.result: Joins and grouping have a target grain.

items.title: Name required sources
items.explanation: List the tables or views containing each fact and the key that relates them.

items.title: Separate filters from grouping
items.explanation: Decide which individual rows qualify and which calculations combine rows.
items.result: WHERE and HAVING have distinct jobs.

items.title: Define ordering and limits
items.explanation: Choose a stable order and a justified page size when the result can be large.
items.result: The output is useful and repeatable.

blocks.prompt: If a query returns rows, does that prove it answered the business question?
blocks.explanation: SQL engines report syntax and execution success, not whether the chosen row meaning, relationship, filters, and ordering match the question.

sections.title: 2. Read rows with SELECT, FROM, and WHERE
sections.summary: Filtering reduces candidate rows; projection chooses which columns the result exposes.

blocks.code:
SELECT id, title, created_at
FROM tickets
WHERE status = 'open'
  AND created_at >= :since
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 50;
blocks.explanation: FROM names the source relation. SELECT projects the requested columns. WHERE keeps rows meeting both predicates. A named parameter supplies a value safely from application code. The second ordering key makes ties deterministic, and LIMIT bounds the result returned.

blocks.title: A query clause answers one question
blocks.caption: Read the clauses as a pipeline of intent, not as decorative keywords.

segments.label: Shape
segments.explanation: Chooses the columns each output row contains.

segments.label: Source
segments.explanation: Starts with rows from the tickets relation.

segments.label: Filter
segments.explanation: Keeps only rows whose status matches the predicate.

blocks.title: Never build SQL by concatenating user input
blocks.body: Use the database driver's parameter binding. It keeps values separate from SQL syntax and is the primary defense against injection for ordinary values.

sections.title: 3. Join tables without changing the question
sections.summary: A join combines rows through a relationship, but the chosen join and key can change row count and meaning.

blocks.text: An inner join keeps only tickets with a matching customer. A left join keeps every ticket and adds customer columns when a match exists. If one ticket can have many tags, joining tags can produce several output rows for one ticket. That multiplication is not automatically wrong; it must match the result grain or be handled with grouping or existence tests.

blocks.code:
SELECT t.id, t.title, c.name AS customer_name
FROM tickets AS t
JOIN customers AS c ON c.id = t.customer_id
WHERE t.status = 'open';
blocks.explanation: Aliases make each column's source clear. The ON condition states the key relationship. Because JOIN is inner here, tickets whose customer_id has no matching customer are excluded; a LEFT JOIN would preserve them for a diagnostic or incomplete-data report.

blocks.prompt: Can adding a one-to-many join leave the number of output rows unchanged?
blocks.explanation: One parent row can match several child rows, producing several joined rows. Check the intended grain before counting, paginating, or displaying the result.

sections.title: 4. Aggregate deliberately, especially around NULL
sections.summary: Grouping changes the row meaning; NULL represents missing or unknown rather than an ordinary value.

blocks.code:
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS open_ticket_count
FROM tickets
WHERE status = 'open'
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY open_ticket_count DESC;
blocks.explanation: WHERE chooses tickets before grouping. GROUP BY creates one result row per customer_id. COUNT(*) counts rows in each group. HAVING filters groups after aggregation; it is not interchangeable with WHERE.

blocks.text: NULL means no known value, so NULL = NULL is not true. Use IS NULL or IS NOT NULL to test it. COUNT(column) ignores NULL values, while COUNT(*) counts rows. COALESCE can supply a fallback for display, but it should not hide a data-quality distinction that the question needs to preserve.

rows: Equality comparisons with NULL do not produce true.
Counts rows, including rows whose selected column is NULL.
Makes an explicit replacement at the result boundary.
blocks.caption: Make missingness part of the question instead of treating it as an empty string.

sections.title: 5. Change data with constraints and transactions
sections.summary: Write operations need a target, a safety condition, and a clear all-or-nothing boundary when several changes belong together.

blocks.text: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes matching rows, and DELETE removes matching rows. A missing WHERE on UPDATE or DELETE can affect every row. Constraints such as primary keys, foreign keys, unique values, and checks reject invalid states at the database boundary. A transaction groups related statements so the database can commit them together or roll them back according to its guarantees.

blocks.explanation: The guarded UPDATE prevents a negative quantity if the predicate is enforced atomically. The application must inspect the affected-row result before inserting the dependent item; on failure it should roll back rather than commit a partial order.

blocks.prompt: Does BEGIN by itself guarantee that an inventory reservation succeeded?
blocks.explanation: A transaction groups work, but the update predicate, affected-row check, constraints, isolation behavior, and commit outcome still determine whether the intended state was achieved.

sections.title: 6. Make retrieval predictable and affordable
sections.summary: Indexes and query plans are workload tools: they can reduce reads for a pattern while adding storage and write cost.

blocks.text: An index is an additional structure organized for selected lookups or ordering. Create one because a measured workload needs it, not because every column should be indexed. A query planner may choose a sequential scan, an index scan, or a join strategy based on statistics and estimated cost. EXPLAIN (or the database's equivalent) shows the chosen plan; compare it with the actual data distribution and latency rather than trusting a slogan.

rows: Does the filter or join have a useful selective access path?
Inspect the plan, statistics, and rows examined.
Is the predicate selective and type-compatible, and is the index order useful?
Check the actual plan and parameter values.
How many structures must each change maintain?
Measure write latency and remove indexes that serve no real workload.
Order by a deterministic key in addition to the visible sort field.
blocks.caption: Performance diagnosis starts with measurements and a representative workload.

sections.title: 7. Debug and operate SQL as a boundary skill
sections.summary: Reliable SQL work includes migrations, permissions, observability, recovery, and evidence when the result is wrong.

items.title: Check the row grain
items.explanation: Count a known key and inspect duplicates introduced by joins.
items.result: You know whether multiplication or grouping is involved.

items.title: Check predicates and NULL
items.explanation: Test each filter independently and inspect missing values explicitly.
items.result: A hidden three-valued-logic case is visible.

items.title: Check the request and parameters
items.explanation: Capture the parameterized statement shape, values, duration, and affected-row count without logging secrets.
items.result: Application and database boundaries can be separated.

items.title: Check schema history
items.explanation: Confirm the deployed migration, constraints, indexes, and database version match the code's assumptions.
items.result: Environment drift is not mistaken for query logic.

blocks.title: Production SQL discipline
items: Review destructive statements with a SELECT using the same WHERE first.
Use least-privilege database roles and parameterized queries.
Apply reversible, ordered migrations and define how large backfills avoid blocking normal traffic.
Record query latency, errors, lock waits, and affected-row counts with sensitive values excluded.
Back up data and rehearse restore; a successful migration is not a recovery plan.

glossary.definition: A set of rows described by named columns; in everyday SQL work it is commonly represented by a table or query result.
A condition that evaluates whether a row or group qualifies for an operation.
An operation that combines rows from relations according to a matching or other relationship condition.
A calculation such as COUNT, SUM, MIN, MAX, or AVG that combines multiple input rows into a value.
The database's chosen strategy for executing a SQL statement, including scans, joins, and ordering work.
A versioned change to database schema or data applied in a known order.
